people.seed: Lutheran farmer, 58, Minnesota, quiet and practical
people.desc: Dale Sorensen farms 900 acres of corn and soybeans outside Litchfield, Minnesota, on land his grandfather broke. He has served two terms on the council of his ELCA congregation, mostly on the building committee, and he reads the Small Catechism the way he reads a seed catalogue: plainly, looking for what it actually says. His younger brother died in a grain-bin accident in 2009 and Dale did not cry at the funeral, which still bothers him more than he tells anyone. He says little at the co-op coffee table, but when he does speak it is usually the dry joke that gets the biggest laugh.

notes.note: He thinks it depends on how well you know them and whether it is any of your business. "It's your job" is stronger than he would put it, so he hedged with Not sure.
Slightly confusing. He values a steady temper and admires people who don't fly off the handle, but a heart that never stirs sounds to him like a man who doesn't care. Not sure was the nearest.
His real answer is "that's God's business, not mine". Not sure covers it, but he would rather have said it is not his to decide.
He believes the stories happened and also that they mean something. He was not sure which the statement wanted him to pick.

people.overall: Easy enough to get through, and most of it was common sense. A few read like questions for a pastor, and he answered those with a shrug.

people.seed: Episcopal librarian and introvert, 44, Oregon, admires monks
people.desc: Ruth Delaney is a reference librarian at the public library in Corvallis, Oregon, married to a high-school chemistry teacher, no children. She grew up in a Pentecostal family in Bakersfield, drifted away in college, and was confirmed in the Episcopal Church at 33 after a friend took her to Compline. Twice a year she makes a silent retreat at the Trappist abbey near Lafayette and is slowly working through the Sayings of the Desert Fathers. She still keeps a dream journal, a habit from her childhood church that she is a little embarrassed about, and she is known at vestry meetings as the quiet one who will not move once she has made up her mind.

notes.note: For her it is true, but the monks she admires live in community on purpose, and she felt the statement set up a false choice. She agreed, but only mildly.
She recognised the idea from the desert monks and is drawn to it, but thinks stillness is not the same as feeling nothing. Agree was the nearest, with reservations.
She does not think being rich is wrong in itself, but she doubts most people manage to use it well. She disagreed mildly because of the camel and the needle, not because of the wording.
She hopes so, with Julian of Norwich, but would never say she knows it. Agree is a little stronger than hope.

people.overall: She enjoyed it, and it felt more thoughtful than most online quizzes. A couple of statements made her want to write a paragraph in the margin.

people.seed: Owner of a small business who attends a prosperity-gospel church, 39, Houston
people.desc: Andre Whitfield owns an HVAC company in Pearland with eleven trucks and a waiting list every August. He attends a large nondenominational church in southwest Houston where the pastor preaches on sowing seed and speaking increase over your life. His mother, a lifelong Missionary Baptist from Fifth Ward, thinks the church is too flashy, and they argue about it every Thanksgiving. He tithes on gross, not net, and is proud of it. He coaches his son's Little League team, listens to business podcasts in the truck, and will lose his temper at a supplier on the phone and then call back ten minutes later to apologise.

notes.note: His answer is "both": it happened AND it means something. He disagreed because "more than what literally happened" sounded like it was calling the miracles stories.
He believes God already did His part and you have to show up and do yours. "Mostly up to you" leaves God out a bit, so he agreed but not strongly.
Gut says yes, but he feels like the right answer in church is no. He split the difference.
Felt slightly loaded to him, like a politics question. He gives a lot and believes in being a blessing, but "really belongs to them" is not how he sees his money.

people.overall: Quick and pretty fun. Most answers came instantly, though a few felt like they were fishing for a political answer.

people.seed: Young Catholic Worker volunteer, 29, Boston, social-justice minded
people.desc: Claire Nguyen lives and works at a Catholic Worker house of hospitality in Boston and covers her own costs with per-diem nursing shifts. Her parents came from Vietnam in 1981 and built a nail salon in Worcester, and they are still hurt that she turned down a full-time hospital job to live in voluntary poverty. She goes to daily Mass, prays the rosary on the bus, and has been arrested once, praying outside a weapons contractor in Andover. She is funny, blunt and usually tired, and she is more traditional on doctrine than her friends from the protest scene expect.

notes.note: She thinks you can only say it if you love the person and have earned the right to. As a flat "it's your job" it sounds like busybody religion, so she landed on Not sure.
Her honest answer is "we may hope so, but the Church doesn't let me say I know". Not sure is near, though it is really a hope rather than doubt.
She reads Scripture in both the literal and the spiritual sense and did not want to rank them. Not sure because both matter, not because she doubts.
She thinks questions about God should be asked, but that some of the answers are mystery. "Left alone" read as "don't ask", which she does not like.

people.overall: It felt good, and she answered most of it strongly and fast. She liked that it asked about money and war, not only belief.

people.desc: Wayne Tillman has been a deacon at First Baptist in a county seat north of Birmingham for twenty-two years. He retired after thirty-one years as a shop teacher and assistant football coach, and every few years he teaches the men's Sunday school class straight through Romans. He hunts deer in November, watches the news more than his wife would like, and fishes most Saturdays with his closest friend, a Black Methodist preacher he met coaching. He is warm, blunt and hard to move, and when a friend died of Covid in 2020 he wept at the graveside without any shame about it.

notes.note: Depends what kind of wisdom. Common sense, sure; wisdom about God, no, since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of it. Not sure was the only way to say "it depends".
He thought of Rahab and Corrie ten Boom and hesitated. Lying is a sin, but he is not sure he'd blame someone hiding Jews from the Nazis.
He believes in church discipline from Matthew 18, but "put out" skips the steps before it. He agreed only mildly for that reason.
He wants prayer in schools and the Ten Commandments on the courthouse wall, but he also knows Baptists fought for the separation of church and state. He agreed, but not strongly.
Slightly confusing: he read it as being about salvation, and so disagreed strongly. He does believe you have to work at living right once you are saved.

people.overall: Mostly clear, and he answered most of it with confidence. A few statements seemed written to catch him out, the money one especially.
